title: Longest substring
description: Sliding window with a Set: expand the right edge, shrink the left while a duplicate sits in the window. O(n) time.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section is what you'd say (or ask) before writing the next chunk of code. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.reveal:
I'd start by repeating the prompt back: "Longest substring of `s` with no repeating characters — by substring you mean contiguous, right? (As opposed to subsequence.)"

Then the cheap clarifying questions:
• Character set — ASCII only, or full Unicode? (Affects the space bound.)
• Empty string — return 0?
• Case sensitivity — is "aA" length 2 or 1?
• What gets returned — the length, or the substring itself? (The function name says length, but worth confirming.)

These take 20 seconds and they signal that you don't just dive in.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n²) solution before you discard it.
sections.reveal:
"The brute force is: for every starting index `i`, walk forward with `j` and track seen characters in a Set. The moment you hit a repeat, record `j - i` and move `i` forward. That's O(n²) time, O(n) space."

Why say this out loud? Two reasons:
1. It proves you understand the problem before optimizing.
2. It plants the seed for the real solution — the brute force is doing redundant work, restarting the Set on every `i`. The optimization is just: don't restart, slide instead.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to sliding window?
sections.reveal:
"Longest contiguous X satisfying a property" is the canonical sliding-window trigger. Two more signals confirm it here:

• The property ("no repeats") is monotone in window shrinkage — if `[l..r]` has a duplicate, removing chars from the left can only fix it, never break it. That means I never have to backtrack `r` once I move it forward.
• I only need O(1) membership checks per char, which a hash set gives me.

So: one pass with `r`, a Set tracking what's in the window, and `l` advances only when forced. Each char enters and leaves the Set at most once → O(n).

sections.title: 4. Walk a small example
sections.reveal:
I'd narrate this on the whiteboard:

  r=0 'a' → seen={a},   window [0,0], best=1
  r=1 'b' → seen={a,b}, window [0,1], best=2
  r=2 'c' → seen={a,b,c}, window [0,2], best=3
  r=3 'a' → duplicate! shrink: delete s[0]='a', l=1. seen={b,c}. add 'a'. window [1,3], best=3
  r=4 'b' → duplicate! shrink: delete s[1]='b', l=2. seen={c,a}. add 'b'. window [2,4], best=3
  r=5 'c' → duplicate! shrink: delete s[2]='c', l=3. seen={a,b}. add 'c'. window [3,5], best=3
  r=6 'b' → duplicate! shrink twice: delete s[3]='a' then s[4]='b'. l=5. add 'b'. window [5,6], best=3
  r=7 'b' → duplicate! shrink: delete s[5]='c'... wait, no — delete s[5]='c'? Let me check. Actually here l=5, s[5]='c'. Delete 'c', l=6. Still duplicate ('b' at s[6]). Delete s[6]='b', l=7. add 'b'. window [7,7], best=3.

Return 3. The trace also exposes the subtle bug: delete s[l] **before** l++, otherwise you delete the wrong char.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.reveal:
Before I declare it done, I'd call these out:

• Empty string → loop doesn't execute, `best` stays 0. ✓
• Single char → r=0, no duplicate, best=1. ✓
• All same char ("aaaa") → each new `r` triggers a full shrink, but each char still enters/exits the set once → O(n). best=1.
• All unique ("abcdef") → `l` never moves, best=n.
• Unicode/surrogate pairs — if the input has emoji, indexing `s[r]` gives you UTF-16 code units, not codepoints. Worth flagging to the interviewer; the fix is `[...s]` to iterate by codepoint.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.reveal:
**Time: O(n).** Each character is added to `seen` at most once and removed at most once. So even though there's a nested `while`, the total work across the whole outer loop is bounded by 2n.

**Space: O(min(n, |alphabet|)).** The Set never holds more than the alphabet size — 128 for ASCII, much smaller in practice. For arbitrary Unicode it's bounded by `n`.

If asked to extend: "At most K distinct chars" → swap the Set for a count-Map and shrink while `map.size > K`. Same template, different shrink condition. That generalization is the reason we used `while` for the shrink instead of `if`.

notes: Window is the substring s[l..r] inclusive — its length is r - l + 1.
Shrink with a while loop so the template generalizes to count-based windows.
Delete s[l] BEFORE incrementing l — otherwise you delete the wrong char.

options: We only need membership (in the window) — uniqueness is implicit
O(n) — each char enters and leaves the window once

questions.q: When the right pointer sees a duplicate, you should:
options: Shrink from the left until the duplicate is removed

exercises.prompt: Fill in the sliding-window with a Set.

L3.prompt: Write `lengthOfLongestSubstring(s)` returning the length of the longest substring without repeating chars. Log `lengthOfLongestSubstring("pwwkew")`.
hints: Slide a window [l, r] across the string.
While the new char is already in the Set, delete s[l] and l++.
Track best = r - l + 1 after each step.
